pos: n. (free imperial city of Franconia, German Nurnberg; the first great imperial city to adopt the Reformation, 1525)
etymology: From German Nurnberg, the rocky hill, from Nuoren berc; Latinised Norimberga.
biblical_def: Nuremberg was the richest and best-governed of the free imperial cities, and it was the first of them to go over wholly to the Reformation, by act of its council in March 1525 after a public colloquy. Its advantages were two: printing presses that had made it a centre of the book trade since the previous century, and a patrician council that moved deliberately rather than by riot. Andreas Osiander preached at St Lorenz; Lazarus Spengler, the city secretary, drafted the documents; Albrecht Durer died there in the city's first evangelical years. The Nuremberg church order of 1533, written with Brandenburg, became a model for Lutheran Germany and reached England through Archbishop Cranmer. The dictionary records Nuremberg for the method as much as the outcome: a city that read first, printed what it read, and then decided. “searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11) is the Berean commendation, and it describes a procedure, not a mood.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines inspiration as the conveying of ideas into the minds of men by supernatural influence, reproof as censure for a fault, and printing as the art of impressing characters on paper.
webster_full: INSPIRATION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the conveying into the minds of men, ideas, notices or monitions by extraordinary or supernatural influence.
REPROOF, n. Blame expressed to the face; censure for a fault; reprehension.
CORRECTION, n. Punishment; discipline; chastisement; that which corrects.
PRINT'ING, n. The art or practice of impressing letters, characters or figures on paper, cloth or other material.
scriptures: These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness:
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,
corruption_summary: The first great free imperial city to reform, 1525; its presses, its council, and the church order of 1533.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern suspicion of deliberate, documented, institutional change, as though only spontaneous movements were sincere. Nuremberg was slow, legal and literate, and it held what it gained for three hundred years while hotter cities lost theirs.

The principle to recover is that conviction is meant to be checked against the text before it is acted on. The Bereans are commended for exactly that: they “received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). The text is sufficient for the work — “All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction” (2Ti 3:16) — and it is to live in a congregation, not in a study only: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom” (Col 3:16). Understanding itself is a gift: “Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luk 24:45).

pos: n. (imperial cathedral city on the Rhine; the Diet of 1529 where the Protestation was entered, giving the name Protestant)
etymology: From German Speyer, from the Speyerbach stream; Latin Spira, English formerly Spires.
biblical_def: Speyer gave the Reformation its common name. The Diet of 1526 had left each prince to order religion as he would answer for it to God and the Emperor, and under that ruling the evangelical territories had built churches for three years. The Diet of 1529 revoked it. On the nineteenth of April six princes and fourteen free cities entered a formal protestation, declaring that in matters touching God's honour and the salvation of souls each man must stand alone before God, and that they could not consent to a decree against the plain word; from that document they were called Protestants. The dictionary records Speyer because the protestation was not a bid for autonomy but an appeal to a higher court. The ground was Peter's: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), and the manner was the three Hebrews' at the furnace — respectful, submissive to every lawful penalty, and immovable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a protest as a solemn declaration of dissent commonly against some act, conscience as the faculty by which we judge the moral rectitude of our own actions, and an appeal as the removal of a cause to a superior tribunal.
webster_full: PROTEST', n. A solemn declaration of opinion, commonly against some act; a formal declaration of dissent.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.
APPEAL, n. The removal of a cause from an inferior to a superior tribunal.
OBEY, v.t. [L. obedio; ob and audio, to hear.] To comply with the commands, orders or instructions of a superior.
scriptures: Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Act 4:19
But Peter and John answered and said unto them, Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye.

And if it seem evil unto you to serve the LORD, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD.
corruption_summary: The Diet of 1529, the Protestation of nineteen April, and the origin of the name Protestant.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the reading of protest as mere dissent, a posture of grievance against authority as such. The men of Speyer were loyal subjects who paid their taxes, kept their oaths and offered their bodies to the Emperor's justice; what they refused was to command their consciences against the word of God.

The principle to recover is that obedience to men is real but bounded, and the boundary is God's revealed command. Peter sets the rule: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29), and he had already put the matter to the council as a question they could not answer: “Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye” (Act 4:19). The furnace shows the temper required, which refuses without defiance and leaves the outcome with God: “be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods” (Dan 3:18). And the choice is finally a household's, not a state's: “as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD” (Jos 24:15).

pos: n. (free imperial city on the Danube; reformed by vote of its citizens in 1530 and ordered by Bucer, Oecolampadius and Blarer)
etymology: From Old High German Ulma, perhaps from a word for a marshy place; Latin Ulma.
biblical_def: Ulm did something few cities did: it put the Reformation to a vote. In November 1530 the citizens entitled to the franchise were polled parish by parish, and by about four to one they resolved to leave the imperial religious settlement and reform the city's worship. The council then did the sensible thing and sent for help, summoning Martin Bucer from Strasbourg, Johannes Oecolampadius from Basel and Ambrosius Blarer from Constance to draft a church order; the resulting ordinance of 1531 regulated preaching, the sacraments, the schools and the care of the poor, and it governed the city for a generation. The dictionary records Ulm because enthusiasm reforms nothing by itself; what endures is an order, written down, by which a church can be examined. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) is a standing apostolic requirement, and Paul left Titus in Crete precisely “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting” (Tit 1:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines order as a methodical arrangement in which things bear a due relation to each other, decent as becoming and proper, and to ordain as to establish, institute or appoint.
webster_full: ORDER, n. Regular disposition or methodical arrangement of things; a state in which things bear a due relation to each other.
DECENT, a. Becoming; suitable; fit to be seen; proper in manner, dress, or language.
ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino, from ordo, order.] To set; to establish; to institute; to constitute; to appoint.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company or collection of individuals, in the same place; usually for the same purpose.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.
Tit 1:5
For this cause left I thee in Crete, that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city, as I had appointed thee:
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: The imperial city that reformed by a citizens' poll in 1530 and took its church order from Bucer, Oecolampadius and Blarer.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the preference for a church shaped by atmosphere and personality rather than by a written order that outlasts the men who wrote it. Ulm's ministers came, drafted, and went home; the ordinance remained, and could be read by anyone who wanted to know what the city believed and how it worshipped.

The principle to recover is that God requires an ordered church, and that the order is part of the obedience. The rule is apostolic: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Supplying what is lacking and ordaining officers is named as the specific commission: “that thou shouldest set in order the things that are wanting, and ordain elders in every city” (Tit 1:5). It is kept by assembling and not otherwise — “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is” (Heb 10:25) — around the four marks of the first church: “the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42).

pos: n. (free imperial city on the Lake of Constance; one of the four cities of the Tetrapolitan Confession, 1530)
etymology: From German Lindau, the island of limes, from Linde, lime tree, and Au, island meadow.
biblical_def: Lindau was a small island city in the Lake of Constance with a large place in one document. At the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 the south German cities could not subscribe the Saxon confession because they would not accept its language on the Lord's Supper, and they would not simply stay silent; so Strasbourg, Constance, Memmingen and Lindau presented their own, the Tetrapolitan Confession, drafted chiefly by Bucer and Capito. It was never adopted as an imperial standard and was superseded within a few years as the cities moved toward the Swiss and then toward concord with Wittenberg, but it was what four small governments did when a confession was demanded and they could neither sign nor dissemble. The dictionary records Lindau for that act. “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven” (Mat 10:32) is not a counsel for the strong only; four lake towns against an empire is the usual scale of it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confession as the acknowledging of the truth and a profession of faith, profession as open declaration and public avowal of one's belief, and a witness as that which furnishes evidence or proof.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. Acknowledgment; the acknowledging of a fault or of the truth; a profession of faith.
PROFESSION, n. The act of professing or claiming; open declaration; public avowal or acknowledgment of one's sentiments or belief.
WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event. That which furnishes evidence or proof.
FAITH, n. The assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed; a firm and cordial belief.
scriptures: For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation.
Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;)
corruption_summary: One of the four cities of the Tetrapolitan Confession at Augsburg in 1530, which would neither subscribe nor stay silent.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern treatment of a confession as a private opinion that need not be stated where stating it costs something, so that belief is held sincerely and never said. The Tetrapolitan cities were offered precisely that escape and refused it.

The principle to recover is that saving faith is confessing faith, and that the confession is public by definition. Scripture binds the two together: “For with the heart man believeth unto righteousness; and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom 10:10). The Lord stakes His own acknowledgment on it: “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father” (Mat 10:32). Paul reminds Timothy that he “hast professed a good profession before many witnesses” (1Ti 6:12), and the charge is to keep it without flinching: “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering” (Heb 10:23).

pos: n. (free imperial city on the Neckar in Swabia; reformed under Ambrosius Blarer, 1531)
etymology: From Old High German Hezzilinga, the settlement of Hezzilo's people; German Esslingen.
biblical_def: Esslingen reformed late and carefully. Evangelical preaching had been heard in the city through the 1520s, but the council hesitated for a decade between the Emperor on one side and its own citizens on the other, and only in 1531 did it call Ambrosius Blarer from Constance to preach and to order the city's churches. Blarer stayed a year and a half, abolished the mass, reorganised the schools and the poor relief, and left behind a settlement the council could administer. The city joined the Schmalkaldic League, and paid for it in the war of 1546. The dictionary records Esslingen because its reformation was the work of a deliberating council rather than a prince or a crowd, which is the ordinary case in the free cities and the harder one to tell as a story. “in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14) is the sober text for such a government, and the standard for choosing the counsellors is given in Exodus: “able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness” (Exo 18:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines counsel as advice given for directing the judgment or conduct, a counsellor as one appointed to advise a king or state, and a magistrate as a public civil officer invested with some branch of the executive government.
webster_full: COUNSEL, n. Advice; opinion or instruction given upon request or otherwise, for directing the judgment or conduct.
COUNSELLOR, n. Any person who gives advice; particularly, one appointed to advise a king or state.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
RU'LER, n. One that governs, whether emperor, king, pope or governor; any one that exercises supreme power over others.
scriptures: Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety.
Pro 24:6
For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war: and in multitude of counsellors there is safety.

Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens:
Pro 29:2
When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice: but when the wicked beareth rule, the people mourn.
corruption_summary: A Swabian imperial city reformed in 1531 by Ambrosius Blarer at the call of a council that had deliberated for ten years.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is impatience with deliberation, which now reads as cowardice or as a failure of conviction. Esslingen's council was slow because it was answerable, and when it moved it moved the whole city and did not have to move it twice.

The principle to recover is that God has appointed counsel as the ordinary means of good government, and character as the qualification for it. The proverb is blunt about the alternative: “Where no counsel is, the people fall: but in the multitude of counsellors there is safety” (Pro 11:14), and it applies to the hardest decisions of all: “For by wise counsel thou shalt make thy war” (Pro 24:6). Jethro's standard is moral before it is administrative: “able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness” (Exo 18:21). And the people feel the difference: “When the righteous are in authority, the people rejoice” (Pro 29:2).

pos: n. (free imperial city of Swabia; evangelical from 1521 under Matthaus Alber, and a signatory of the Augsburg Confession)
etymology: From Old High German Rutilinga, the people of Rutilo; German Reutlingen.
biblical_def: Reutlingen was among the earliest imperial cities to hear evangelical preaching and among the firmest in holding it. Matthaus Alber, a native of the town, preached there from 1521 and remained for nearly forty years; he was the man to whom Zwingli addressed his first open letter on the Lord's Supper, and he stood against the Anabaptists who worked the Swabian countryside without conceding anything to the sacramental party either. The city subscribed the Augsburg Confession in 1530, joined the Schmalkaldic League, was fined and occupied after the war of 1547, and kept its evangelical order anyway. The dictionary records Reutlingen because steadiness in one place over four decades is the least dramatic and most productive form of ministry there is. “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58) is addressed to such men, and so is the warning against the opposite temper: “Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines” (Heb 13:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stedfast as firmly adhering, constant and resolute, grace as favour and good will, and faith as the assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed.
webster_full: STED'FAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; firmly adhering to; constant; resolute.
GRACE, n. Favor; good will; kindness; disposition to oblige another.
FAITH, n. The assent of the mind to the truth of what God has revealed; a firm and cordial belief.
DOCTRINE, n. Principles or positions in any science; whatever is taught; that which is held, put forth as true, and supported by a teacher.
scriptures: Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.
Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle.
Php 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
Heb 13:9
Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines. For it is a good thing that the heart be established with grace; not with meats, which have not profited them that have been occupied therein.
corruption_summary: Evangelical from 1521 under Matthaus Alber, who held one pulpit for forty years against Rome, Anabaptism and the Emperor alike.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption that a long ministry in a small place is what happens to men who could not get a larger one. Alber had the ear of Zwingli and the confidence of an empire city, and he spent his life in the town he was born in.

The principle to recover is that endurance in one charge is itself the fruit, and that it is secured by holding what was delivered rather than by seeking what is new. The apostolic charge is to immovability: “be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1Co 15:58). What is to be held is what was taught: “stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle” (2Th 2:15). The congregation stands with its minister — “that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel” (Php 1:27) — and the opposite is named as a drifting: “Be not carried about with divers and strange doctrines” (Heb 13:9).

pos: n. (free imperial city on the Main; the empire's book fair, and host of the exiled English congregation of 1554)
etymology: From German Frankfurt, the ford of the Franks; Latin Francofurtum.
biblical_def: Frankfurt was the trading crossroads of the empire, the city where emperors were elected and where twice a year the book fair gathered printers from every country in Europe; what was printed in Geneva or Basel reached Poland and Scotland through Frankfurt. It reformed in 1533, and in the following decades it took in Dutch and Walloon refugees from the Netherlands and, in 1554, the English congregation fleeing Mary. That congregation then tore itself apart over the Book of Common Prayer in the quarrel known as the troubles at Frankfurt, which sent Knox back to Geneva and sowed the seed of English Puritanism. The dictionary records Frankfurt as the Reformation's great entrepot of books and exiles, and as a warning that a city may be generous to strangers while the strangers are ungenerous to one another. “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers” (Heb 13:2) is the city's commendation; the quarrel inside its walls is the other half of the record.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines hospitality as the practice of receiving and entertaining strangers without reward, a stranger as a foreigner not entitled to the privileges of a citizen, and a fair as a stated market in a particular town.
webster_full: HOSPITALITY, n. The act or practice of receiving and entertaining strangers or guests without reward.
STRANGER, n. A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one not entitled to the privileges of a citizen.
FAIR, n. A stated market in a particular town or city; the wares sold at such a market.
PRINT'ING, n. The art or practice of impressing letters, characters or figures on paper, cloth or other material.
scriptures: Heb 13:2
Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in:
Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality.
corruption_summary: The empire's book fair and a refuge for Dutch, Walloon and English exiles; and the scene of the troubles at Frankfurt, 1554.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern reduction of hospitality to a temperament — warmth, welcome, a certain style of greeting — rather than the costly practice of housing people who have nowhere else to go. Frankfurt housed whole congregations with their ministers, their presses and their poor.

The principle to recover is that receiving the stranger is commanded, and that it is done to Christ. The command stands without qualification: “Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares” (Heb 13:2). Israel was bound to it by the memory of its own exile: “the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you” (Lev 19:34). The Lord counts it as done to Himself — “I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35) — and Paul names it among the ordinary duties of a congregation: “Distributing to the necessity of saints; given to hospitality” (Rom 12:13).

“I was a stranger, and ye took me in” (Mat 25:35) — and the troubles at Frankfurt, 1554.

pos: n. (free imperial city of Swabia; reformed in 1522, and the field of the Protestant defeat of 1634)
etymology: From Old High German Nordilinga, the people of the north settlement; German Nordlingen.
biblical_def: Nordlingen is two things in the record. It was one of the first imperial cities to reform, under Theobald Billicanus from 1522, a quiet Swabian town that put down the mass early and kept its evangelical order through the century. And it is the name of the battle fought outside its walls in September 1634, when the Swedish and German Protestant army was destroyed by the imperial and Spanish forces, a defeat that ended Protestant dominance in southern Germany and drove France into the war. The dictionary records Nordlingen because the pairing is instructive and uncomfortable: the same city stands for an early, clean, popular reformation and for the military catastrophe that nearly undid it. Faith does not guarantee the field. “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7) is not a promise of victory in every battle; it is the discipline of where to put one's confidence when the battle is lost.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines war as a contest between nations carried on by force, a battle as an engagement between opposing armies, and to trust as to place confidence in or rely on.
webster_full: WAR, n. 1. A contest between nations or states, carried on by force, either for defense, or for revenging insults and redressing wrongs.
BATTLE, n. A fight or encounter between enemies, or opposing armies; an engagement.
CHARIOT, n. A half coach; a carriage with four wheels; a car used anciently in war.
TRUST, v.t. To place confidence in; to rely on.
scriptures: Psa 20:7
Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God.
Isa 31:1

Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because they are many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the LORD!

And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God's.
Psa 46:9
He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth; he breaketh the bow, and cutteth the spear in sunder; he burneth the chariot in the fire.
corruption_summary: Reformed under Billicanus in 1522, and the field of the 1634 defeat that ended Protestant dominance in southern Germany.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the half-believed assumption that God underwrites the arms of the side that holds the better doctrine, so that defeat becomes evidence against the doctrine. Nordlingen was a Protestant city and a Protestant disaster in the same hundred years.

The principle to recover is that the Lord disposes of battles and is not a party to them, and that confidence belongs to His name and not to the means. The contrast is stated plainly: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psa 20:7). Alliances sought in place of that trust are named a woe: “Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots” (Isa 31:1). The ownership of the contest is His: “for the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15), and the end of all such contests is His doing: “He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth” (Psa 46:9).
roots_summary: Hebrew milchamah (H4421), battle or war; Hebrew batach (H982), to trust or lean upon.
roots_lines: Hebrew rekeb (H7393) — a chariot, the strength men trust in; Psalm 20:7.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to call to mind deliberately; Psalm 20:7.
Hebrew shaan (H8172) — to lean upon, to stay oneself on; Isaiah 31:1.
Hebrew milchamah (H4421) — war, battle, the engagement itself; 2 Chronicles 20:15.
Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cause to cease, to make to rest; Psalm 46:9.
usage: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses” (Psa 20:7) — Billicanus and the reformation of 1522.
“for the battle is not yours, but God's” (2Ch 20:15) — the field outside the walls, September 1634.
“He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth” (Psa 46:9) — a defeat that drew France into the war.

pos: n. (free imperial city of the Allgau; reformed in 1525, with a Catholic prince-abbot ruling the adjoining territory)
etymology: From Latin Cambodunum, the Roman town on the Iller; German Kempten.
biblical_def: Kempten is the sharpest example in Germany of two jurisdictions on one piece of ground. The free imperial city reformed in 1525 and remained evangelical; immediately outside its gates the prince-abbot of Kempten ruled a Catholic territory from his own abbey, and for nearly three hundred years the two governments, one Protestant and one Roman, divided a single small valley between them. They quarrelled over tolls, over jurisdiction, over which bells might be rung, and they both survived until Napoleon dissolved them together. The dictionary records Kempten because it is the Reformation's plainest picture of the two swords held by different hands, and of the obligation that rests on the Christian in such a case: to honour the lawful authority over him without yielding to it the conscience that belongs to God. “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a ruler as one that governs and exercises supreme power over others, subject as placed or situate under, and honour as the esteem due or paid to worth.
webster_full: RU'LER, n. One that governs, whether emperor, king, pope or governor; any one that exercises supreme power over others.
SUBJECT, a. — Placed or situate under.
HONOUR, n. 1. The esteem due or paid to worth; high estimation; respect; veneration.
MAGISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
scriptures: They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
Pro 21:1
The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will.
corruption_summary: An evangelical imperial city and a Catholic prince-abbot sharing one valley for three centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs two ways. One error makes the civil ruler a matter of indifference, as if a Christian owed him nothing at all; the other makes him the arbiter of worship, as if submission in civil things carried submission in sacred ones. Kempten had to answer both questions every day.

The principle to recover is the division the Lord Himself drew, which grants the magistrate a real but bounded claim. The ruling is exact: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21). Civil authority is genuinely from God: “there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). The duties are listed in their order and are not interchangeable: “Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king” (1Pe 2:17). And the ruler himself is governed: “The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1).
roots_summary: Greek exousia (G1849), authority; Hebrew leb (H3820), the heart turned by the LORD.
roots_lines: Greek apodidomi (G591) — to render, to give back what is owed; Matthew 22:21.
Greek exousia (G1849) — authority, delegated power; Romans 13:1.
Greek hupotasso (G5293) — to be subject, to range oneself under; Romans 13:1.
Greek timao (G5091) — to honour, to value at a price; 1 Peter 2:17.
Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the seat of a king's purpose; Proverbs 21:1.
usage: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's” (Mat 22:21) — city and prince-abbot in one valley.
“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — three centuries of tolls, jurisdiction and bells.
“The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD” (Pro 21:1) — both governments dissolved together under Napoleon.

pos: n. (free imperial city on the Neckar; reformed under Johann Lachmann, and seat of the Protestant league of 1633)
etymology: From German Heilbronn, the holy spring, from heilig and Brunnen.
biblical_def: Heilbronn took its name from the spring under its church and gave its name to a covenant. Johann Lachmann, its preacher from 1524, carried the city into the Reformation without the violence that convulsed the Swabian countryside in the peasants' rising, and the city was formally evangelical from 1530. A century later, in April 1633, the Swedish chancellor Oxenstierna gathered the Protestant estates of four south German circles there and bound them into the Heilbronn League, a confederation to carry on the war after the death of Gustavus Adolphus; it was broken at Nordlingen the next year. The dictionary records Heilbronn because both halves of its history turn on the word covenant, and because Scripture makes the difference between a covenant entered before God and an alliance merely signed. Josiah “made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments” (2Ch 34:31); the Heilbronn League was an instrument of policy, and lasted eighteen months.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a covenant as a mutual agreement of two or more persons to do or forbear some act, a league as an alliance between states for mutual defence, and an alliance as a union of interests between nations or parties.
webster_full: COVENANT, n. [L. con and venio, to come together.] A mutual consent or agreement of two or more persons, to do or to forbear some act or thing; a contract; stipulation.
LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.
ALLIANCE, n. A union or connection of interests between nations or parties, often condemned in the prophets when made in place of trust in God.
SEAL, n. A piece of metal or other hard substance, usually round or oval, on which is engraved some image or device, and used to make an impression on wax.
scriptures: And the king stood in his place, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments, and his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and with all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant which are written in this book.
And they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul;
And Jehoiada made a covenant between the LORD and the king and the people, that they should be the LORD'S people; between the king also and the people.
Jer 50:5
They shall ask the way to Zion with their faces thitherward, saying, Come, and let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten.
corruption_summary: Reformed under Johann Lachmann from 1524, and the seat of Oxenstierna's Protestant league of April 1633.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the flattening of covenant into contract, so that a solemn engagement before God is treated as a negotiated instrument that lapses when its advantages do. The Heilbronn League was exactly such an instrument and behaved exactly as such instruments behave.

The principle to recover is that a true covenant is made before the LORD, binds the heart, and has His commandments for its content. Josiah's is the pattern: he “made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments” (2Ch 34:31). Asa's generation bound themselves in the same terms: “they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers with all their heart” (2Ch 15:12). Jehoiada joined ruler and people under it — “that they should be the LORD'S people” (2Ki 11:17) — and the prophet looks for one that does not expire: “let us join ourselves to the LORD in a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten” (Jer 50:5).
roots_summary: Hebrew berith (H1285), a covenant cut; Hebrew darash (H1875), to seek with care.
roots_lines: Hebrew berith (H1285) — a covenant, a compact cut and sworn; 2 Chronicles 34:31.
Hebrew karath (H3772) — to cut, used of making a covenant; 2 Kings 11:17.
Hebrew darash (H1875) — to seek, to enquire after diligently; 2 Chronicles 15:12.
Hebrew halak (H1980) — to walk, to order one's life; 2 Chronicles 34:31.
Hebrew olam (H5769) — perpetual, age-enduring; Jeremiah 50:5.
usage: “made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD” (2Ch 34:31) — Lachmann and the city, evangelical from 1530.
“they entered into a covenant to seek the LORD God of their fathers” (2Ch 15:12) — the estates assembled under Oxenstierna, April 1633.
“a perpetual covenant that shall not be forgotten” (Jer 50:5) — the league broken at Nordlingen eighteen months later.
